name: ground_highway
prompt:
One image is attached: finished art from the same top-down 2D city game, at one scale. Top row, left to right: a square of the town's road asphalt (its fresh look above, its worn look below), a square of the town's footway asphalt, a square of its grass; below them two cars, 4.5 m long. Match that art's look: crisp, clean hand-painted game art, natural colours, tidy and well kept. It must NOT look like a photograph: no blur, no photographic noise.

Make one image of 12 separate squares of ground texture, in a 4 by 3 grid — 3 rows of 4, read left to right and top to bottom — each square the same size, a clear gap of transparency between neighbouring squares and from the picture's edge. They are the ground of an intercity highway running out of town: its carriageway's asphalt and the gravel shoulder beside it. The game repeats each over large areas, under cars, turned at any angle.

The highway's asphalt (rows 1 and 3) must read clearly as a different, more important road than the town's road in the attached picture when the two meet at a junction: clearly darker — near black, where the town's is charcoal grey — and newer.

Shape comes first:
- Each square is filled edge to edge, right into all four corners: no border, frame, rim, bevel, outline, shadow or vignette, and its edges look the same as its middle.
- Outside the squares the background is fully transparent. No text, numbers, labels or grid lines anywhere.

Rules for every square:
- Look straight down (orthographic). No perspective, no light falling off towards any edge.
- Each square is 9.2 × 9.2 m of ground. Keep everything true to size: a stone of the shoulder one to three centimetres, a chip of the asphalt about a centimetre.
- How each asphalt square is built: a smooth, even surface whose grain is fine — small specks a pixel or two across, so close together that they read as one texture and never as separate stones — with only gentle, soft, broad variations of tone. No pebbles you can pick out one by one, no rubble, cracks, potholes, patches or oil blotches: it is in good repair.
- No direction and no pattern: no joints, seams, lines, stripes, ruts, tyre tracks, grooves, brush strokes or grid of any kind, so the square looks the same turned any way.
- Even texture: the same tone and density all over the square, nothing that catches the eye, so it repeats without a visible pattern.
- The four squares of a row are the same ground: exactly the same colours, grain and style, so they can be joined without a visible seam. The first two of a row are its fresh look; the last two the same ground a little more used.
- Nothing stands on the ground and nothing is painted on it: no road markings, paint, lines, kerbs, drains, posts, plants, litter or objects.

Row 1 — cells 1 and 2: new highway asphalt: deep near-black binder, clearly darker than the town road in the attached picture, with a slightly coarser grain than it: tightly packed small dark grey chips about a centimetre across, embedded flat, with a few pale ones among them. Cells 3 and 4: the same highway asphalt a little more used: a shade less black, the same chips, soft faint lighter patches of tone where tyres have polished it. No oil spots, no cracks.

Row 2 — cells 5 and 6: a gravel road shoulder: compacted grey-beige crushed stone fines packed hard and flat, densely scattered small grey and buff stones one to three centimetres across, soft broad patches of slightly darker packed earth. Cells 7 and 8: the same gravel shoulder a little more used: drier and dustier, a shade browner, more packed earth showing between the stones, still flat. No plants, no grass, no puddles.

Row 3 — cells 9 and 10: fresh smooth black asphalt with a faint cool blue-black tint, very even, a fine tight grain of tiny dark grey specks and very few pale ones — also clearly darker than the town road in the attached picture. Cells 11 and 12: the same smooth black asphalt a little more used: a shade greyer, soft faint lighter patches. No oil spots, no cracks.
